The language has 5 phonemic tones, marked on every vowel in the IPA here.

Stress falls on the next-to-last syllable.
Core words average 1.94 syllables (3.7 sounds); 18% of words share their form with another word.

## Orthography

The house romanization in two registers: the full spelling (workbench, one letter or digraph per sound, tone marks) and the book spelling (lossy: no tone, plain vowels, at most one diacritic letter a word).

**Consonants:** m ‹m› · n ‹n› · ŋ ‹ng› · p ‹p› · t̪ ‹t̪› ‹t› · t ‹t› · k ‹k› · ʔ ‹'› · ʈʰ ‹ṭ› · z ‹z› · ʃ ‹sh› · h ‹h› · ɬ ‹hl› · ɮ ‹dl› · ɻ ‹ḻ› · j ‹y› · w ‹w› · j‼ ‹yrh› · l ‹l› · r ‹rr› · ɾ‼ ‹rrh›

**Vowels:** i ‹i› · i‼ ‹irh› · ɨ ‹ï› · u ‹u› · u‼ ‹urh› · eː ‹ee› · o ‹o› · ə‼ ‹erh› · ɜ̠ ‹ë̠› ‹e› · ɜ̠‼ ‹erh› · ɐ ‹a› · a ‹a›

Tones are written over the vowel: low grave à, mid unmarked a, high acute á, rising caron ǎ, falling circumflex â (Yoruba-style).

Where two spellings are given the second is the book spelling.

## Grammar

Basic word order is SOV; it has postpositions. In the noun phrase: possessor before the possessed; noun before the adjective; demonstrative before the noun; noun before the numeral; relative clause before the noun. Overall it is head-final.
It has a definite article before the noun, no indefinite article, no case marking on nouns, nominative-accusative alignment, no grammatical number, no gender or noun classes.
Verbs mark perfective and habitual; there is an indirect (reported or inferred) evidential. Negation uses a negator before the verb; yes/no questions use intonation alone. Verbs agree with the subject by suffixes; not with the object.
Other features: pronouns can be dropped; alienable and inalienable possession told apart; a copula; a periphrastic causative; no passive; question words moved to the front; a vigesimal counting base; locational possession ('at me is a dog').
Measured morphology: 12 live grammatical markers, mean bondedness 0.6 (0 free word … 3 fused), 8 paradigm cells, 1 of them with allomorphy.

### Grammar sketch

Built from the typology and the live markers above (planet/language/sentences.py); where the engine tracks no marker for a construction, the form is the word such markers commonly grow from, and the text says so. Examples are glossed by the Leipzig rules (abbreviations under Sample sentences).

**Number.** Nouns do not mark number: one noun form serves for one or many; a numeral or 'many' says how many.

**Case.** Nouns have no bound case. Adpositions (free words, not yet case): locative (LOC): a separate word after the noun phrase (j‼i˧, from 'head'); dative (DAT): a separate word after the noun phrase (ɻi˧, from 'give'). The typology leans nom-acc in alignment, but no case marker shows it yet: word order tells subject from object.

| *ti˧hi‼˧* | *j‼i˧* |
| --- | --- |
| house | LOC |

‘in the house’

| *ʔji˧li˧* | *ɻi˧* |
| --- | --- |
| man | DAT |

‘to/for the man’

**Gender and noun classes.** There is no gender or noun class.

**Tense and aspect.** Verbs mark tense and aspect. Imperfective (IPFV): a separate word after the verb (ə‼˧j‼, from the progressive marker); habitual (HAB): a separate word after the verb (i˧ɜ̠˧, from 'know'). Unmarked: past, future, progressive (left to context).

| *ɜ̠˧u‼˧ɾ‼* | *ə‼˧j‼* |
| --- | --- |
| go | IPFV |

‘(it) is going’

| *ɜ̠˧u‼˧ɾ‼* | *i˧ɜ̠˧* |
| --- | --- |
| go | HAB |

‘(it) usually goes’

**Mood and evidentiality.** Speakers mark how they know: reported (evidential) (REP): a separate word after the verb phrase (u˧, from 'say').

| *ɜ̠˧u‼˧ɾ‼* | *u˧* |
| --- | --- |
| go | REP |

‘(it) goes, they say’

**Person agreement.** Verbs agree with the subject: 1PL: a clitic after the verb (i‼˨, from 'person'); 2PL: a suffix (pɐ˦, from 'you'); 3PL: a suffix (ŋɨ˦, from 'they'). Subject pronouns are dropped when the marker is there. No marker yet for 1SG, 2SG, 3SG (zero).

| *ɜ̠˧u‼˧ɾ‼=i‼˨* |
| --- |
| go=1PL |

‘we go’

| *ɜ̠˧u‼˧ɾ‼-pɐ˦* |
| --- |
| go-2PL |

‘you all go’

| *ɜ̠˧u‼˧-ŋɨ˦* |
| --- |
| go-3PL |

‘they go’

**Negation.** Negation is a separate word before the verb phrase (nwjɜ̠˧li˧, from 'nothing'); the typology calls it preverbal.

| *i˧* | *ŋɨ˦=ha˧ri˧* | *nwjɜ̠˧li˧* | *ru˨˦* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1SG | DEF=milk | NEG | drink |

‘I do not drink the milk.’ (sentence 6 below)

**Questions.** Yes/no questions use rising intonation alone. Question words move to the front: who ɾ‼ə‼˧ri‼˧, what ɾ‼ə‼˧ri‼˧, where pjɜ̠˧, when ɨ˨h, how pu‼˦hu‼˦.

| *ŋi˦ri˧ɜ̠˧ŋ* | *ŋɨ˦=ti‼˧ʔa˦˨ku˧* | *t̪ɐ˦* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2SG | DEF=thunder | hear |

‘Do you hear the thunder?’ (sentence 4 below)

| *ɾ‼ə‼˧ri‼˧* | *ŋɨ˦=ji˧pa˧ʔi˧* | *ɜ̠˧u‼˧ɾ‼mu˨* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| what | DEF=child | bring |

‘What does the child bring?’ (sentence 5 below)

**Possession.** The possessor stands before the possessed noun, with no marker. Kin and body parts (inalienable) take no genitive marker. 'Having' is said with a locational phrase ('at my mother is a dog').

| *ŋɨ˦=ʔji˧li˧* | *li˧* |
| --- | --- |
| DEF=man | dog |

‘the man's dog’

| *i˧* | *kɜ̠˧* | *j‼i˧* | *ku˦ʈʰa˦li˧j‼* | *t̪ji˧* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1SG | mother | LOC | boat | COP |

‘My mother has a boat.’ (sentence 7 below)

**Relative clauses.** Relative clause before the noun, no relativizer.

| *ru˨˦i˧rɜ̠‼˧ŋ* | *ŋɨ˦=krɜ̠‼˧* |
| --- | --- |
| dance | DEF=woman |

‘the woman who dances’

**Copula.** The copula is the word for 'he, she, it' (G056).

| *hu˧ŋu‼˧lɜ̠‼˧lu‼˧* | *ʔji˧li˧* | *i˦ru˧ɻi˧* | *t̪ji˧* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| that | man | merchant | COP |

‘That man is a merchant.’ (sentence 9 below)

| --- | --- | --- |
| DEF=water | cold | COP |

‘the water is cold’

### Families a historian reconstructs

The roots a historian reconstructs: every word's family as it was when the word was made, carried forward however opaque it has become since (per-word `etym_roots`, the *bher- 'carry' > burden view). 59 families of 3+ words; 56% of the 715 words share a root with another word.

## Sample sentences

Built from this language's own words, word order, markers and agreement (planet/language/sentences.py). Each has the form line (‘-’ an affix boundary, ‘=’ a clitic boundary), a morpheme-by-morpheme gloss, the free translation, then the whole sentence in IPA (after the simple joining rules: a glide between two vowels, a nasal taking the place of a following stop) and in the book spelling. Nothing here is attested speech; it is what the grammar data implies.
